items.title: Most fresh water on Earth is locked in ice
items.claim: Where is most of Earth's freshwater?

options.text: Around 68% of freshwater is in glaciers and ice caps; around 30% is groundwater; surface water (rivers, lakes, wetlands) is under 1% of freshwater and about 0.01% of all water on Earth

items.reveal:
Earth's total water: around 97.5% saline (oceans), 2.5% fresh. Of that 2.5%: glaciers and ice caps around 68%, groundwater around 30%, surface and atmospheric water under 2%.

Groundwater is the world's largest accessible freshwater store but is being depleted in many regions (the Ogallala Aquifer, the North China Plain, parts of India). NASA GRACE satellites have mapped the depletion.

The Aral Sea, once the world's fourth-largest lake (68,000 km²), shrank by 90% from 1960 by Soviet irrigation diversions — one of the most visible water-management failures of the 20th century.
items.why: Water scarcity is partly a storage problem. Most freshwater is inaccessible (ice, deep aquifers); we depend on a tiny fraction — surface water and shallow aquifers — that is unevenly distributed and vulnerable.

items.title: A tsunami can cross the Pacific in under 24 hours
items.claim: How fast does a tsunami travel in deep ocean?

options.text: Around 30 km/h, comparable to wind waves
Around 700-900 km/h in deep ocean (calculated as √(g × depth)) — jet airliner speed; the 1960 Chile tsunami reached Hawaii (10,000 km away) in about 15 hours and Japan in around 22 hours
The speed of sound in water (around 5,400 km/h)
A fixed 100 km/h regardless of depth

items.reveal:
Tsunami speed in open ocean depends on depth: at 4,000 m, around 700 km/h; in 50 m, around 80 km/h. As the wave shoals at coasts, energy compresses vertically and the wave grows from under a metre to potentially tens of metres.

The 1960 Chilean earthquake (M9.5) generated a Pacific-wide tsunami: Hawaii saw 10 m waves around 15 hours later; Japan, 17,000 km away, saw 5 m waves 22 hours after. 142 people died in Japan from a Chilean earthquake.

The Pacific Tsunami Warning Center (Honolulu, 1949) uses DART buoys (Deep-ocean Assessment and Reporting of Tsunamis) to detect pressure changes from passing waves.
items.why: Distance gives time for warning across ocean basins — but not for nearby coasts. The 2004 Sumatran tsunami killed locally in minutes; Sri Lanka had two hours; Somalia had seven. Warning systems must work at all timescales.

items.title: Aftershocks can be larger than the original quake
items.claim: What is the technical relationship between a mainshock and aftershocks?

options.text: Aftershocks are always smaller than the mainshock

If a later event is larger than the original, it is retrospectively reclassified as the mainshock and the earlier event becomes a foreshock — so by definition the named mainshock is the largest in the sequence
Aftershocks are unrelated to mainshocks and randomly distributed

items.reveal:
Bath's law gives the largest aftershock as typically 1.2 magnitudes smaller than the mainshock. Omori's law (1894) gives the rate as decaying as 1/t. Aftershocks can continue for years after large events.

The 2011 Christchurch earthquake (magnitude 6.3, 22 February) was an aftershock of the September 2010 Darfield earthquake (7.1). Because the Christchurch event was smaller, it kept the aftershock label — but it killed 185 people because it was shallower and closer to the city.
items.why: Naming conventions can obscure danger. The aftershock label can sound like 'less hazardous' when the geometry of the event matters more than its magnitude.
